nameStory: The bulbous buttercup gets its name from the swollen, bulb-like base of its stem that sits just below ground level. This chunky underground storage organ helps the plant survive tough conditions and gives it a distinctive 'bulbous' look that sets it apart from its many buttercup cousins. Some folks also called it 'St. Anthony's turnip' because that rounded base reminded them of a small turnip.
description: Bulbous buttercup is a low-growing perennial wildflower that brightens New England fields and lawns with cheerful bright yellow flowers in late spring and early summer. This compact plant typically reaches 6-12 inches tall and has deeply divided, three-lobed leaves that emerge from the base on long stems. The glossy yellow flowers have five petals that shine like they've been polished with butter, giving all buttercups their memorable name. What makes this species special is its swollen stem base that acts like a underground storage bulb.

idTips.label: Stem Base
idTips.description: The stem has a distinctive swollen, bulb-like base just at or below soil level that feels firm and rounded when you gently brush away dirt - this is the key feature that separates it from other buttercups

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers with five glossy, waxy-feeling petals that reflect light like tiny mirrors, typically about an inch across with numerous yellow stamens in the center

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided basal leaves cut into three main lobes, each lobe further divided, giving them a lacy, delicate appearance - leaves feel slightly fuzzy and emerge on long stems directly from the base

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, compact plant forming small clumps rather than spreading widely, with flowers held on stems that rise above the cluster of basal leaves

habitat: Look for bulbous buttercup in disturbed areas like old fields, pastures, roadsides, and weedy lawns throughout New England. It thrives in well-drained soils and full sun to partial shade, often appearing in areas that have been grazed or mowed. You'll frequently find it mixed with other common field flowers like dandelions and clover.

seasonality.spring: Basal leaves emerge early and flowers begin blooming in late spring, typically May into early June. This is the best time for identification when the distinctive bulbous stem base and fresh flowers are most visible.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade by midsummer and the plant may go dormant in hot, dry weather. Leaves often wither back, making identification more challenging.
seasonality.fall: New basal leaves may emerge in fall if conditions are favorable. The bulbous base remains firm underground even when top growth dies back.
seasonality.winter: Plant is dormant with only the underground bulbous stem base surviving. Above-ground parts are gone, making identification impossible until spring.

funFact: The bulbous buttercup's swollen stem base can actually 'jump' out of the ground when the soil freezes and thaws repeatedly - frost action pushes the bulb upward, which is why you sometimes find these plants sitting on top of the soil in early spring like little botanical popcorn kernels!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with meadow buttercup and creeping buttercup, but neither has that telltale swollen stem base. Memory trick: 'Bulbous base for bulbous buttercup' - if you don't feel that firm, rounded bulge at the stem bottom, it's probably a different buttercup species.
contextualKnowledge: Like all buttercups, this plant contains compounds that make it toxic to livestock and can cause skin irritation in sensitive people. The name 'buttercup' comes from an old belief that cows eating these flowers produced the richest, yellowest butter - though in reality, cattle usually avoid them because of their bitter taste.
compareHints: Among New England's many buttercup species, bulbous buttercup is the only one with that distinctive swollen stem base. Meadow buttercup grows much taller with a normal stem, while creeping buttercup spreads by runners along the ground. Early buttercup blooms earlier but lacks the bulbous base and has different leaf shapes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buttercups, small-flowered buttercup is unmistakable due to its tiny petals - all other buttercup species have much more prominent yellow flowers.
Among New England's buttercups, hooked buttercup is unique for its woodland habitat and tiny, pale flowers—most other buttercups prefer sunny, open areas and have much brighter, larger yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercup species, meadow buttercup stands out for its tall, upright growth and deeply palm-divided leaves.
Unlike meadow buttercup which grows in upright clumps, or bulbous buttercup with its swollen stem base, creeping buttercup is the only common buttercup that spreads by runners along the ground.
Unlike other New England buttercups that have bright, showy yellow flowers, cursed crowfoot has tiny, pale, almost insignificant blooms.
Among New England buttercups, bristly crowfoot stands out for its rough, hairy texture and pale flowers - most other buttercups have smoother leaves and bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercups, yellow water-crowfoot is one of the few truly aquatic species, distinguished by its floating stems and dramatic leaf differences between air and water.
Among New England's buttercups, creeping spearwort is unique for its simple, narrow leaves - all other local buttercups have divided or lobed leaves.
Unlike the robust meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup with their typical three-lobed leaves, fen crowfoot has leaves so finely divided they look almost thread-like.

Among New England's many buttercups, early buttercup stands out for its combination of very early bloom time, preference for dry rather than moist habitats, and distinctively narrow, deeply-cut leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which grows tall and robust in fields, Allegheny Mountain buttercup stays much smaller and more delicate.
Rock buttercup stands out from other New England buttercups by having the smallest, palest flowers in the family - most other buttercups have bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among the 20+ buttercup species in New England, lesser spearwort stands out immediately because of its narrow, spear-shaped leaves – all other buttercups have lobed, divided, or rounded leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which prefers drier ground and grows much taller, swamp buttercup stays low and spreads along wet soil.
Among New England's aquatic buttercups, longbeak buttercup is distinguished by its exceptionally long fruit beaks and preference for flowing water.

Among New England's many buttercups, bristly buttercup stands out primarily for its rough, hairy texture - most other species like meadow buttercup and creeping buttercup have relatively smooth stems and leaves.

Unlike terrestrial buttercups like meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup, small yellow water-crowfoot is adapted for aquatic life with thicker, more succulent leaves and a strictly prostrate growth habit.
Unlike all other New England buttercups that grow upright, Lapland buttercup stays completely flat and creeping.
Among New England's many buttercups, water-plantain spearwort is unique for its completely undivided, lance-shaped leaves - most other buttercups have deeply lobed or divided leaves.
Unlike its terrestrial buttercup cousins that have typical yellow flowers, thread-leaved water-crowfoot has white petals with yellow centers and specialized underwater foliage.
